this_file: Curated essential 60 hymns with full metadata and scripture anchors
notes: Charles Wesley wrote approximately 6,500 hymns. These 60 represent the essential doctrinal and devotional canon — the hymns that shaped Methodist worship and Protestant hymnody broadly. All public domain.

hymns.title: O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing
hymns.first_line: O for a thousand tongues to sing
hymns.theme: The praise that overflows from the converted heart — never enough tongues
hymns.history: Written on the first anniversary of Charles's Aldersgate experience (May 21, 1739). The original 18-stanza poem began with stanza 7 of the modern version. 'My gracious Master and my God' is the original opening.

brother_parallel.note: Written the same year John published Salvation by Faith. Both respond to Aldersgate.

hymns.title: Hark! The Herald Angels Sing
hymns.first_line: Hark! the herald angels sing
hymns.theme: The cosmic significance of the incarnation — not just birth but redemption
hymns.history: Original first line: 'Hark how all the welkin rings / Glory to the King of Kings.' George Whitefield changed it to the familiar version. Charles was reportedly displeased. The theology of stanza 2 ('Veiled in flesh the Godhead see') is among the finest incarnation poetry in English.

hymns.title: Christ the Lord Is Risen Today
hymns.first_line: Christ the Lord is risen today
hymns.theme: The Easter triumph — death swallowed up in victory
hymns.history: Originally titled 'Hymn for Easter Day.' The 'Alleluia' at the end of each line was added later by editors, not Charles. Remains the most sung Easter hymn in English.

hymns.title: Love Divine, All Loves Excelling
hymns.first_line: Love divine, all loves excelling
hymns.published_in: Hymns for those that Seek and those that Have Redemption (1747)
hymns.theme: The arc from God's love entering the heart to the full perfection of the new creation
hymns.history: Intentionally echoes John Dryden's 'Fairest Isle' — claiming the tune and meter for sacred use. The controversial stanza ('Take away our bent to sinning') encodes Wesley's doctrine of entire sanctification. Final stanza ('Finish then thy new creation') sometimes sung as a separate hymn.

brother_parallel.note: Written same year as John's mature Christian Perfection sermon — same doctrine in two registers.

hymns.title: And Can It Be That I Should Gain
hymns.first_line: And can it be that I should gain
hymns.theme: Astonishment that Christ died for me — the personal wonder of substitutionary love
hymns.history: Written within days of Charles's Aldersgate experience, May 1738. The prison-door imagery in stanza 4 ('My chains fell off, my heart was free') directly mirrors John Wesley's own prison imagery in his Aldersgate account. Both brothers wrote the same metaphor independently the same week.

brother_parallel.shared_imagery: prison chains broken — both brothers used this image for their Aldersgate moments

hymns.title: Jesus, Lover of My Soul
hymns.first_line: Jesus, lover of my soul
hymns.theme: The soul fleeing to Christ in the storm — nearer to thee is safety
hymns.history: One of the most beloved hymns in the English language. John Wesley initially refused to publish it — thought the phrase 'lover of my soul' too intimate. It was published after Charles insisted. Ironic given it became more beloved than almost anything John wrote.

hymns.title: Soldiers of Christ, Arise
hymns.first_line: Soldiers of Christ, arise
hymns.theme: Putting on the full armor of God — each piece named and applied
hymns.history: A verse-by-verse exposition of Ephesians 6:10-18 in hymn form. Wesley was doing what he always did — turning doctrine into song so it could be memorized and sung by people who couldn't read.

hymns.title: Arise, My Soul, Arise
hymns.first_line: Arise, my soul, arise
hymns.theme: Christ our great High Priest intercedes — therefore approach the throne boldly
hymns.history: The five wounds of Christ named in each stanza. Each stanza presses toward assurance: 'His Spirit answers to the blood / And tells me I am born of God.'

hymns.title: Come, Thou Long Expected Jesus
hymns.first_line: Come, thou long expected Jesus
hymns.published_in: Hymns for the Nativity of Our Lord (1745)
hymns.theme: Israel's long messianic longing finding its fulfillment — and our own longing for His return
hymns.history: Originally a two-stanza Advent hymn. The second stanza ('Born thy people to deliver') makes the connection between the first Advent and present salvation explicit.

hymns.title: Rejoice, the Lord Is King
hymns.first_line: Rejoice, the Lord is King
hymns.theme: The ascended Christ reigns — therefore rejoice and shout

hymns.title: Forth in Thy Name, O Lord, I Go
hymns.first_line: Forth in thy name, O Lord, I go
hymns.theme: All ordinary labor consecrated as divine calling
hymns.history: Written the year Charles married Sarah Gwynne and began settling into domestic life rather than itinerant preaching. The hymn reads as a theology of vocation for those whose ministry is the ordinary world — his own situation.
hymns.biographical_context: Written as Charles transitioned from itinerant to settled life

hymns.title: O Thou Who Camest from Above
hymns.first_line: O thou who camest from above
hymns.published_in: Short Hymns on Select Passages of Holy Scripture (1762)
hymns.theme: The sacred fire kindled at conversion to burn as perpetual offering
hymns.history: A meditation on Lev 6:13 — the fire that must never go out on the altar. Wesley applies it to the fire of divine love in the heart. Often called his finest single stanza of all.

brother_parallel.note: Written year before John's Scripture Way of Salvation — both reaching doctrinal maturity

hymns.title: Lo, He Comes with Clouds Descending
hymns.first_line: Lo, he comes with clouds descending
hymns.published_in: Hymns of Intercession for All Mankind (1758)
hymns.theme: The return of Christ — universal sight, universal response
hymns.history: Based on an earlier hymn by John Cennick (1752). Charles revised and expanded it. The combined version is superior to either original — a rare collaboration Wesley had with another hymnwriter.

hymns.title: Depth of Mercy! Can There Be
hymns.first_line: Depth of mercy! can there be
hymns.theme: The mercy that receives the returning sinner — even after relapse
hymns.history: Significant because it addresses relapse — the believer who has fallen again. Wesley doesn't romanticize the fall but insists on the depth of mercy that still waits. Pastoral and honest.

hymns.title: Come, Sinners, to the Gospel Feast
hymns.first_line: Come, sinners, to the gospel feast
hymns.theme: The universal gospel invitation — no one excluded, everyone called
hymns.history: Wesley's response to Calvinist limited atonement. The hymn insists the invitation is genuinely universal: 'Come, all the world; come, sinner, thou.' The atonement is sufficient for all.

hymns.title: O Come and Dwell in Me
hymns.first_line: O come and dwell in me
hymns.published_in: Short Hymns on Select Passages of Holy Scripture (1762)
hymns.theme: The prayer for Christ to dwell within and complete his transforming work

hymns.title: Come, Holy Ghost, Our Hearts Inspire
hymns.first_line: Come, Holy Ghost, our hearts inspire
hymns.theme: The Spirit who inspired Scripture now illuminates the reader of Scripture
hymns.history: A Pentecost hymn specifically about the Spirit's work in opening Scripture — the same Spirit who breathed the Word now breathes understanding. Distinct from later 'Spirit of God Descend' which is by George Croly.

hymns.title: Where Shall My Wondering Soul Begin
hymns.first_line: Where shall my wondering soul begin
hymns.theme: The convert's first response — what do I say? Where do I begin? Go tell everyone.
hymns.history: The very first hymn Charles Wesley ever published, written immediately after his Aldersgate experience, May 1738. The poem is addressed outward — calling others to come to the same grace he just found. The convert's first instinct is to evangelize.
hymns.historical_significance: First Charles Wesley hymn ever published

hymns.title: Captain of Israel's Host, and Guide
hymns.first_line: Captain of Israel's host, and guide
hymns.published_in: Short Hymns on Select Passages of Holy Scripture (1762)
hymns.theme: The Exodus as pattern for the believer's pilgrimage — guided by cloud and fire

hymns.title: O Love Divine, What Hast Thou Done
hymns.first_line: O love divine, what hast thou done
hymns.theme: Astonishment at substitutionary love — the Immortal dying for me

hymns.title: Victim Divine, Thy Grace We Claim
hymns.first_line: Victim divine, thy grace we claim
hymns.theme: Christ present in the Lord's Supper as the once-for-all Victim now perpetually offered
hymns.history: From the 166-hymn collection 'Hymns on the Lord's Supper' (1745) — Wesley's most sustained theological project. These hymns represent the deepest theological poetry Charles produced. The collection as a whole argues for a high view of the Supper without transubstantiation.

brother_parallel.note: Both brothers insisted on the Supper as genuine means of grace, against Quaker spiritualism

hymns.title: Maker, in Whom We Live
hymns.first_line: Maker, in whom we live
hymns.published_in: Hymns of Petition and Thanksgiving for the Promise of the Father (1746)
hymns.theme: The three Persons of the Trinity each addressed as restoring the image of God

hymns.title: God of All Power, and Truth, and Grace
hymns.first_line: God of all power, and truth, and grace
hymns.theme: The great petition: make us partakers of the divine nature — entire sanctification

hymns.title: O For a Heart to Praise My God
hymns.first_line: O for a heart to praise my God
hymns.theme: The longing for a pure heart — the prayer that precedes entire sanctification

hymns.title: Jesus, United by Thy Grace
hymns.first_line: Jesus, united by thy grace
hymns.theme: Christian fellowship as participation in the unity of the Trinity
hymns.history: A hymn about the Methodist class meeting — Wesley understood Christian formation as communal, not individual.

hymns.title: Light of the World, We Hail Thee
hymns.first_line: Light of the world, we hail thee

hymns.title: Eternal Beam of Light Divine
hymns.first_line: Eternal beam of light divine
hymns.theme: Christ as the eternal brightness of the Father's glory

hymns.title: Christ, Whose Glory Fills the Skies
hymns.first_line: Christ, whose glory fills the skies
hymns.theme: Morning prayer: Christ as Sun of Righteousness filling the dark soul with light
hymns.history: One of the finest morning hymns in the language. The 'cheerless, joyless' opening describes the inner state before devotion — the hymn moves from darkness to light within its own stanzas.

hymns.title: All Thanks Be to God
hymns.first_line: All thanks be to God

hymns.title: Thou Hidden Source of Calm Repose
hymns.first_line: Thou hidden source of calm repose
hymns.theme: Christ as the hidden source beneath all outward circumstance

hymns.title: Father of Everlasting Grace
hymns.first_line: Father of everlasting grace

hymns.title: Talk with Us, Lord
hymns.first_line: Talk with us, Lord, thyself reveal
hymns.theme: The Emmaus road as pattern for every encounter with the risen Christ

hymns.title: Gentle Jesus, Meek and Mild
hymns.first_line: Gentle Jesus, meek and mild
hymns.history: Written as a children's hymn — one of the first Christian hymns specifically for children in English. The simplicity is intentional, not accidental. Widely criticised later as sentimental but within context is genuinely profound.

hymns.title: Hymn for Christmas Day (Let Earth and Heaven Combine)
hymns.first_line: Let earth and heaven combine
hymns.published_in: Hymns for the Nativity of Our Lord (1745)
hymns.theme: The mystery of the condescension — the Infinite compressed into the finite

hymns.title: All Glory to God in the Sky
hymns.first_line: All glory to God in the sky
hymns.published_in: Hymns for the Nativity of Our Lord (1745)

hymns.title: Weary of Wandering from My God
hymns.first_line: Weary of wandering from my God
hymns.theme: The prodigal's return — addressed to the believer who has wandered

hymns.title: Blow Ye the Trumpet, Blow
hymns.first_line: Blow ye the trumpet, blow
hymns.theme: The Year of Jubilee as type of evangelical freedom and final trumpet

hymns.title: Love's Redeeming Work Is Done
hymns.first_line: Love's redeeming work is done
hymns.theme: Easter: the finished work of redemption vindicated in resurrection

hymns.title: See How Great a Flame Aspires
hymns.first_line: See how great a flame aspires
hymns.theme: The fire of revival spreading — 'O that the world might taste and see'

hymns.title: Granted Is the Savior's Prayer
hymns.first_line: Granted is the Savior's prayer

hymns.title: A Charge to Keep I Have
hymns.first_line: A charge to keep I have
hymns.published_in: Short Hymns on Select Passages of Holy Scripture (1762)
hymns.theme: The solemn charge entrusted to every soul — keep it unto death

hymns.title: Jesus, Thine All-Victorious Love
hymns.first_line: Jesus, thine all-victorious love
hymns.theme: The prayer for love's consuming fire to purify completely

hymns.title: Come on, My Partners in Distress
hymns.first_line: Come on, my partners in distress
hymns.theme: Fellow travelers on the narrow way — press on together

hymns.title: Happy the Souls to Jesus Joined
hymns.first_line: Happy the souls to Jesus joined
hymns.theme: The blessedness of those united to Christ — happiness defined

hymns.title: Servant of All, to Toil for Man
hymns.first_line: Servant of all, to toil for man

hymns.title: O God of All Grace
hymns.first_line: O God of all grace

hymns.title: Shall I, for Fear of Feeble Man
hymns.first_line: Shall I, for fear of feeble man
hymns.theme: Against the fear of man that silences witness

hymns.title: Hymn to the Holy Ghost (Come, Holy Ghost, All-Quickening Fire)
hymns.first_line: Come, Holy Ghost, all-quickening fire
hymns.theme: Petition for the Spirit's reviving fire

hymns.title: I Know That My Redeemer Lives
hymns.first_line: I know that my Redeemer lives
hymns.theme: Job's defiant hope applied to Christian assurance — I know

hymns.title: The Beatitudes (Blessed Are the Poor in Spirit)
hymns.first_line: Happy are they that mourn
hymns.history: A verse expansion of the Beatitudes — a companion piece to John's Sermon on the Mount series preached the same year.

brother_parallel.note: Written the same year as John's Sermon on the Mount series — twin treatments of the same text

hymns.title: How Happy Is the Pilgrim's Lot
hymns.first_line: How happy is the pilgrim's lot
hymns.history: Written as Charles was settling down — a meditation on the freedom of the itinerant who owns nothing and owes nothing. Irony: his most powerful statement of pilgrim freedom written as he stopped being one.

hymns.title: In Age and Feebleness Extreme
hymns.first_line: In age and feebleness extreme
hymns.theme: Dying grace — strength made perfect in weakness
hymns.history: Dictated from his deathbed to his wife Sarah. His last composition. He died March 29, 1788. The final lines: 'In hope of thy arrival, where / The weary wanderers cease from pain.' John survived him by three years.
hymns.historical_significance: Charles Wesley's final hymn, dictated on his deathbed

hymns.title: Away with Our Fears
hymns.first_line: Away with our fears

brother_parallel.note: Same text — both brothers address the transition from spirit of bondage to spirit of adoption

hymns.title: Granted Is the Dying Groan
hymns.first_line: Granted is the dying groan

hymns.title: Savior of All, What Hast Thou Done
hymns.first_line: Savior of all, what hast thou done

hymns.title: Head of Thy Church Triumphant
hymns.first_line: Head of thy church triumphant

hymns.title: Come, Let Us Rise with Christ Our Head
hymns.first_line: Come, let us rise with Christ our Head

hymns.title: Hymn for Pentecost (Spirit of Burning)
hymns.first_line: Granted is the Savior's prayer

hymns.title: O What Shall I Do My Savior to Praise
hymns.first_line: O what shall I do my Savior to praise
hymns.history: The psalmist's question applied to the convert: what can I render? Nothing sufficient — yet the attempt is itself worship.

hymns.title: All Praise to Our Redeeming Lord
hymns.first_line: All praise to our redeeming Lord
hymns.theme: The Methodist class meeting and society as the body of Christ in microcosm
